questions.prompt: What is a plain object best suited for?
options: Storing values under named keys (key/value pairs)
Counting how many properties something has
questions.explanation: Objects map names (string or symbol keys) to values, e.g. { name: 'Ali', age: 30 }. For ordered, numerically indexed data an array is the better fit; for counting entries or arbitrary key types, a Map is often nicer than a plain object.

questions.prompt: What does this expression evaluate to?
questions.explanation: typeof null is "object" — a bug from the very first JavaScript implementation that was kept for backwards compatibility. null is really its own primitive type, so check for it with value === null.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a built-in data property of every array?
questions.explanation: length is a data property that is always one more than the highest index, and it updates automatically as you add elements. size is what Map and Set use; arrays have no count or limit property.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a real typeof result for numeric values in JavaScript?
questions.explanation: JavaScript has no separate int/float/long types: ordinary numbers (both 42 and 4.2) are 64-bit floating point values of type "number". Since ES2020 there is also a second numeric primitive, bigint (e.g. 42n), for arbitrarily large integers.
Arrays are a kind of object, so typeof returns "object" — there is no "array" typeof result. Use Array.isArray(value) to check for an array.

questions.prompt: What is the main difference between an array and a plain object?
options: Array indexes start at 0, object keys start at 1
Arrays store values by numeric position; objects store values by named key
Arrays can only hold strings and numbers
questions.explanation: Both can hold any kind of value and neither has a practical size difference. An array keeps values in numbered, ordered positions starting at 0 (and tracks length); an object is a collection of named properties.
